identification.summary: Microsoft assesses Strawberry Tempest (formerly DEV-0537, also known as LAPSUS$) as a cybercriminal actor that uses a pure extortion and destruction model without deploying ransomware payloads [S1]. It began with targets in the UK and South America and expanded globally, with early attacks hitting cryptocurrency accounts [S1]. The US Cyber Safety Review Board (CSRB) reported in August 2023 that Lapsus$ and related actors relied mainly on simple techniques such as SIM swapping and phishing of employees [S2].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft's March 2022 post does not state a first-observed date [S1]. MITRE describes the group as active since at least mid-2021 [S7]. Brazilian police tied the Ministry of Health breach to December 2021 [S5].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Strawberry Tempest (renamed from DEV-0537 in an April 2023 update to Microsoft's naming taxonomy) [S1]. Microsoft's mapping also lists SLIPPY SPIDER (CrowdStrike) and LAPSUS$ [S8]. MITRE tracks LAPSUS$ as G1004 [S7]. The CSRB reviewed 'Lapsus$ and related threat groups', so some activity it describes may not belong to the Microsoft-tracked cluster [S2].

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor is asserted in the cited sources. Microsoft assesses the actor as cybercriminal [S1]. Those arrested and convicted in the UK were teenagers [S3][S4].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft MSTIC 'assesses' the objective as elevated access for data theft and destruction, often leading to extortion; it gives no formal confidence level [S1]. Arrests in the UK (March 2022) and Brazil (October 2022) and UK convictions (2023) are law-enforcement and court outcomes reported by press [S3][S4][S5].
attribution.basis: Microsoft incident response and telemetry [S1]; CSRB review of the group's attacks (reported by press) [S2]; press reporting on police arrests and sentencing [S3][S4][S5].

objectives: Financial gain through data theft, extortion and, in some cases, destruction of victim systems and resources; Microsoft notes some victims were extorted and others had data leaked publicly without an extortion attempt [S1]. Early attacks targeted cryptocurrency accounts to drain holdings [S1].

sectors: IT services and support firms (to reach partners and suppliers)
regions: United Kingdom and South America (initial focus) [S1]
targeting.notes: Sector and region lists come from Microsoft [S1]; the Brazil example comes from press reporting on the Federal Police investigation [S5].

capabilities.summary: Initial access relied heavily on credentials and social engineering: Redline password stealer, purchased credentials and session tokens, paying employees or partners for credentials and MFA approval (including installing AnyDesk), searching public code repositories for exposed credentials, SIM swapping, personal-email takeover to reset corporate credentials, MFA prompt spamming and session token replay [S1]. Targeted access paths included VPN, RDP, VDI (including Citrix) and identity providers such as Azure AD and Okta [S1]. After access, the actor used AD Explorer, searched SharePoint, Confluence, JIRA, GitLab, GitHub, Teams and Slack for credentials, exploited unpatched JIRA, GitLab and Confluence servers, and used DCSync, Mimikatz and ntdsutil [S1]. In cloud tenants it created global admin accounts, set a mail transport rule to forward organization mail to an actor account, removed other global admins, created virtual machines as attack infrastructure and joined devices to Azure AD [S1]. It deleted on-premises (VMware vSphere/ESXi) and cloud resources, often after exfiltration, and joined victims' incident response and crisis calls [S1]. It used VPS infrastructure and NordVPN egress points matched to target geography to avoid impossible-travel detections [S1]. The CSRB concluded the group mostly used simple techniques and that SIM swapping was central, noting a lucrative SIM-swap criminal market [S2].

campaigns.name: Brazilian Ministry of Health breach
campaigns.summary: Press reports that attackers deleted files, data and instances, affecting the National Vaccination Certificate site; the group claimed 50 TB stolen; records were restored two days later and full restoration took about a month. Brazil's Federal Police later arrested a suspect in October 2022 (Operation Dark Cloud).

campaigns.name: Okta third-party support compromise
campaigns.summary: Per a secondary summary, Lapsus$ accessed Okta systems on 21 January 2022 via a third-party support engineer's account; Okta confirmed on 25 January and later said two customers were affected. Details vary across sources.

campaigns.name: Microsoft, Nvidia, Samsung and Ubisoft incidents
campaigns.summary: Microsoft says the actor claimed access to Microsoft and exfiltrated some source code; Microsoft states one account with limited access was compromised and no customer code or data was involved [S1]. A secondary summary dates Nvidia (late February), Samsung (4 March) and Ubisoft (confirmed 10 March) incidents [S6].

campaigns.name: Microsoft publishes DEV-0537 analysis
campaigns.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence and Incident Response publish TTPs, with detection and hunting guidance added 24 March 2022.

campaigns.name: UK arrests of seven suspects
campaigns.summary: City of London Police report seven people aged 16 to 21 arrested and released under investigation; press reported a 16-year-old from Oxford as alleged leader, though police did not confirm whether he was among those arrested.

campaigns.name: Brazil arrest (Operation Dark Cloud)
campaigns.summary: Brazilian Federal Police arrest a suspect in Feira de Santana, Bahia, linked to the Ministry of Health breach, citing criminal organization and computer intrusion charges among others.

campaigns.name: CSRB review published
campaigns.summary: The Cyber Safety Review Board publishes its review of Lapsus$ and related groups, finding simple techniques and SIM swapping central and criticizing SMS/voice MFA and third-party risk management.

campaigns.name: UK sentencing
campaigns.summary: Arion Kurtaj receives an indefinite hospital order (venue reported inconsistently across sources); a 17-year-old co-defendant receives an 18-month Youth Rehabilitation Order.

diamond.adversary: Financially motivated extortion and destruction actor; arrests and convictions involved teenagers in the UK and a suspect in Brazil [S1][S3][S4][S5].
diamond.capability: Credential theft, purchased access, SIM swapping, MFA fatigue, help-desk social engineering, cloud tenant takeover and resource deletion [S1][S2].
diamond.infrastructure: Dedicated VPS infrastructure and NordVPN egress points chosen to match victim geography; attacker-created VMs inside victim cloud environments [S1].
diamond.victim: Technology, telecom, government, media, healthcare, education, energy, retail and manufacturing organizations, plus IT service providers used as stepping stones [S1].
diamond.socioPolitical: Profit and notoriety; the actor publicly claimed breaches and joined victim incident calls [S1].
diamond.technology: Reliance on SMS/voice MFA, telecom SIM-swap exposure, identity providers, VPN/VDI access, help desks, and internet-exposed JIRA, GitLab and Confluence [S1][S2].

gaps: No state sponsorship is claimed; relevance to DoD is as a disruptive criminal and insider-recruiting threat.
The CSRB report itself (a CISA PDF) was not opened; findings come from press coverage of it [S2].
Microsoft gives no first-observed date or formal confidence level [S1].

Attribution of specific incidents (Okta, Nvidia, Samsung, Ubisoft, Rockstar) to the Microsoft-tracked cluster versus related groups relies on secondary summaries and was not verified against primary vendor or victim statements [S6].
The Brazil arrest and UK convictions concern individuals; their exact roles within the cluster are not established in the sources gathered [S3][S4][S5].
Current activity after 2023 is not covered by the gathered sources.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the identity and access layer: identity providers, VPN/VDI, help desks, cloud tenant admin roles and SMS-based MFA tied to mobile carriers [S1][S2]. Contractor and BPO support staff are also terrain because the actor targets IT service providers to reach partners [S1]. STEP 2: The environment favors the actor where SMS/voice MFA, outsourced support and exposed collaboration/code servers exist [S1][S2]. STEP 3: Observed model is credential theft or purchase, MFA fatigue or SIM swap, admin takeover, data exfiltration, then deletion and extortion, with presence on victim response calls [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is data theft and extortion against contractors and technology or telecom suppliers in the defense supply chain. MDCOA is cloud tenant takeover with admin lockout and mass resource deletion at a mission-critical provider [S1]. Candidate indicators: bursts of MFA prompts, new global admin accounts, mail transport rules forwarding to external addresses, impossible-travel masked by geo-matched VPN egress, VMs created in tenants, and help-desk password-reset requests for privileged users [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track identity-provider and cloud-admin audit events across mission and contractor tenants [S1]. (2) Authorities: this is criminal activity, so coordinate through law-enforcement and DC3/DIB channels as applicable rather than assuming a military response. (3) Mission assurance: protect against destructive deletion with offline backups and break-glass admin accounts, since the actor removed other admins and deleted resources [S1]. (4) Coordination: include help desks, mobile carriers and contractors in exercises, and move from SMS/voice MFA toward phishing-resistant methods as the CSRB recommended [S2].

provenance.importedSummary: LAPSUS$ is cyber criminal threat group that has been active since at least mid-2021. LAPSUS$ specializes in large-scale social engineering and extortion operations, including destructive attacks without the use of ransomware. The group has targeted organizations globally, including in the government, manufacturing, higher education, energy, healthcare, technology, telecommunications, and media sectors.
